THOTH is a strikingly, unapologetically minimalist game. Its visuals are abstract, clean, yet surreal in their colouring; its soundtrack is unearthly, ominous dark ambient; it contains no semblance of story, setting, instructions on how to play, or any words at all really; its gameplay is a relatively threadbare iteration on its chosen genre, but one that's turned on its head by a single clever twist.

The game is a top-down twin stick shooter in which every level is an arena no bigger than your screen populated by relatively small numbers of simple enemies. You shoot a sort of projectile machine gun at them to whittle their health down; once you've done that to every enemy the level is won and you move on to the next, but if you ever let any of them touch you, you die. So far this could describe any of hundreds of games, and in many ways it feels and plays like a horde survival game reduced to a micro scale: small arena, few enemies (though sometimes large in size) and the same struggle for space. 

The twist comes from the fact that in this game enemies do not really "die". When their health is depleted they continue to move or chase you exactly as before, only your bullets now pass through them, but they remain every bit as dangerous otherwise. It's such a simple mechanic with serious consequences on how levels actually play out, forcing you to rethink your approach to movement and combat, because unlike most games you are no longer neutralising threats and gaining breathing room for yourself with each kill. Instead tension and danger remain constant throughout any given level, from start to finish. Speaking of which, the levels themselves are fairly quick as well as varied. They benefit from the gradual introduction of various mechanics, enemy types, environmental quasi-puzzles and even a few bosses, making for a game that never grows stale, while also standing out as a fresh experience.

THOTH is really cool. It's elegant in its minimalism, well thought out, and intuitive in its abstraction even as it never explicitly teaches you any of its mechanics but trusts you to figure it all out for yourself...

I am 32 years old.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.

Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.

With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.

After realizing this, I turned off the game and went back to work. My hand hurt a lot, but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so sorry for myself and became the father I needed to be at that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving like.

Today, I am close friends with the mother of my children. We don't fight, argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents and friends.

Now I have 3 children. My third child is, wait, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my separation, and we just unexpectedly stumbled into each other's lives. We have been dating for a year and are very happy together.

Moral of the story: you never know what life has in store for you, and if I had given up when all odds were against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

At first blush, THOTH looks like a fun game about shooting and avoiding simple geometric shapes. But it is in fact about self-loathing and evading responsibility. See, the shapes you think you need to direct your anger at and destroy, just want to hug you. They are actually your personal relationships that, once destroyed become a gaping hole in your soul that you must avoid contemplating at all costs or the guilt will swallow you. You must skillfully dodge any accountability whatsoever, dancing around to whatever position benefits you best at the moment, only to abandon it as soon as it no longer serves your purposes. 

As the levels advance, relationships become more complex with shifting boundaries that you will violate because you failed to recognize them. Those of family, friends, teachers, lovers, co-workers, and ultimately society itself. You are given plenty of second chances, but you usually still blow it when it matters most.
You are your own worst enemy, and at the end once you have succeeded, all you have gained is solitude.

REVIEW #64
THOTH
----------

THOTH is an arcade-style twin-stick shooter with a very minimalist visual style. However, that is the ONLY thing about this game that is minimalist. Every aspect of this game, outside of its simplistic geometric aesthetic, has some level of depth to it, and after spending a few hours with this game, I'm left very impressed with how the developer managed to carefully balance everything and create a really addictive game that's surprisingly as satisfying to play as it is to conquer.

A good place to start explaining THOTH's depth is its basic rules. To complete a level, all enemies on-screen must be shot until the color is depleted out of them. An enemy that is left partially damaged will quickly heal itself if not promptly finished off. Once an enemy has been conquered, it not only stays in play but also moves faster, tracks the player more aggressively, and cannot be affected by the player's shots in any way. Combine this with how the player's quick movement speed slows down when shooting, and it becomes remarkably easy to trap one's self against the level geometry with a handful of enemies bearing down on you. Because of this, it's necessary to use quick thinking regarding when to shoot or hold fire, when to take an enemy out since they'll become faster, should the enemies on-screen be defeated in a certain order, etc.

THOTH features a 64-level main campaign which is sectioned into 4-level chunks. Completing a chunk without dying twice in a single level acts like a save point, allowing you to bypass that section whenever you like. Dying twice in a level, however, causes you to start at the beginning of that level set again. Each set introduces new obstacles, enemies and level elements, and even after beating the game, I found it fun to see what was coming next. After completing the main campaign, there is additional, randomized level sets that require the player to survive more levels in a row to succeed.

In my opinion, there's no aspect of THOTH that wasn't designed to near perfection. Difficulty ramps up appropriately, controls feel properly responsive, and the sound is really well done, especially the creepy, droning ambiances that work for background music. There's even a local co-op mode, and this combined with the game's bright color palette gives the game a very "Atari 2600 game" feel. If I had any complaint at all, it would be that one or two of the ambiance tracks in the background are a little too abrasive and took me out of the moment.

In conclusion, don't be fooled by THOTH's simplistic looks. There's very deep arcade action here that will test your reflexes as much as your ability to think on your feet. I really enjoy coming back to this game time and again.

If the last game (140) can be compared to playing drums in a rhythm, this one is more of a dance that you have to perform, over and over, till mastery is achieved. It has more room for error but keeps the tension up. You are never safe - enemies are always coming for you. And they cannot be eliminated.

It turns the usual formula upside down - instead of becoming easier towards the final enemy kill in the room, the game becomes harder. Enemies stop getting damage and become faster upon death. Because of this, each level ends with a tense moment, difficulty slowly rising with each fallen shape. The idea is even incorporated in the level replay system - each level gives you two chances to win it, but the second one is a bit harder, because now you cannot touch the walls. You are still punished for failure, not thrown into easy mode.

The whole aesthetic is somehow pleasing to me. Menu does not exist, but I never needed it. Levels are nothing more than several colors and shapes, mainly squares and circles, but it is more than enough to tell how far you progressed and understand the situation. There are no settings, but I never needed them - I just start the game and click the level I wanted to play, without any loading screens, hints or pauses. Death is nothing but a chance to try again, start the segment over, you don't need to wait and are one click away from restart. It has no story or even a single word is written or said, but does it need that? I feel that you know the answer by this point.

Sometimes you meet an enemy that will not appear again in another level. It serves it purpose and is gone. Not being recycled, not returning with higher level or more hit points and neither being the boss of the segment. It feels fresh and makes appreciate itself, leaving an impression of being thoroughly thought out. The writer wanted to say something, said it, and not it is over. No sequel, no TV adaptation, just a pure experience he offers you to try. Even amount of levels - 64 - makes me feel like the game is saving bits to store the level count while at the same time using them to their fullest. It wants to feel complete. Maybe it is.

THOTH becomes more that it seems to be by removing things and combining them in other ways. Even better, it does not bother to include stuff that does not help achieve its goal. I wish more games were like that.

I was not going to recommend this game, until I read the negative reviews and gained an appreciation for it. The need to complete 4 levels in succession adds tension and the repetition of level adds an element of pattern memorisation and puzzle solving. 

The reason I wasn't going to recommend the game is that I usually don't like minimalist aesthetics. To quote Kitty Horrorshow "the appeal of video games for me is that they put you somewhere" and where THOTH chooses to puts you is a textureless void with the level number plastered over the background. The best games combine inventive gameplay with immersion, and THOTH at partly manages the first.

Overall, it's a slightly interesting game with nowhere near enough meat to justify the full asking price.

But I had fun enough with the game and it was pretty satisfying to beat 12 levels in a row, so I also kinda get why it's designed the way it is. But if you buy it be prepared to feel more than a little annoyed.

Liked: A monolithic theme cascading from the menu to the gameplay (even when losing in gameplay...by it focusing on the enemy mechanics rather than the stats of lives or points in a HUD, it gave a mood similar yet different to other cyber-based shooters). Since I have yet to try the coop with someone, I cannot say how the coop is.  This may also be a game that can motivate Unity users to make more creative projects within a familiar genre.

Disliked: Probably the levels with the dotted lines. Though I understood afterwards and adapted (plus with the extra speed noticed with tinkering with how my character moves with and without shooting), it briefly reminded me of some asymetric gameplay where I lost some of the fun (and ya....lost most of the time). Maybe change the dotted line to a similar color of the enemies when one is fully shot (the black with stars void) to signify that the player can't go in but the enemies can.

Thank you for THOTH. Refreshing game. Recommending game.
